VFM&SA Value for Money and Specialised Audits WGEA INTOSAI Working Group on Environment Audit WGEI INTOSAI Working Group on Audit of Extractive Industries Page 7 strategic report FOREWORD The Office of the Auditor General (OAG) as a body corporate has the statutory function to conduct financial, Value for Money, specialized, forensic investigations, and other audits as provided for by the National Audit Act, 2008. This guarantees that the office provides independent assurance to Parliament concerning issues of accountability,transparency and probity in the public finances. Relatedly the statutory function enables the OAG to determine how economically, efficiently, and effectively public bodies have used the resources given to them, in a way that satisfies Parliament and the citizens of Uganda. In line with our vision ‘A Model Supreme Audit Institution that adds value to society’, it is our utmost desire to present quality reports to Parliament, to facilitate oversight and promote accountability during the 2020-2025 Strategic period. I am pleased to introduce the Office of the Auditor General’s fourth Strategic Plan 2020-2025 which covers five (5) financial years from July 2020 to June 2025. This Plan builds on the achievements of the earlier Corporate Plan 2016-2021. In the effort to align the the 2016-2021 Strategic Plan to the National Development Plan III, there was a reduction of the implementation period which meant that all targets could not be achieved. The unachieved targets have now been moved to the 2020-2025 Strategic Plan. This Strategic Plan reflects the office’s ambition to deliver audits that add value to society in line with ISSAI 12 which supports the Value and benefits of Supreme Audit Institutions. Our focus for the next five years is to enhance organizational performance for impactful audits which will make a difference to the lives of citizens. Our audit orientation in this strategic plan is to enhance our capacity, improve audit systems and support structures, and improve audit value addition in providing service delivery for the citizenry. To successfully implement the new strategic plan, which is aligned to National Development Plan III, OAG will rely on strong leadership, staff commitment and effective utilization of the Management Information System. This strategic plan will be effectively monitored through our monitoring and evaluation function during the implementation period. John F. S. Muwanga AUDITOR GENERAL Page 8 strategic report EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The Office of the Auditor General (OAG) is a body corporate established by the National Audit Act 2008 and is headed by the Auditor General appointed under Article 163(1) of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda as amended. Article 163(3) of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda and Sections 13 to 18 of the National Audit Act 2008, mandate the Auditor General to audit and report to Parliament on the accounts of all public offices, including the courts, central and Local government administrations, universities and public institutions of like nature, and any public corporations or other bodies established by an Act of Parliament. The OAG strategic plan 2020-2025 was developed in compliance with the National Development Plan III (NDP III) and sets out the strategic direction to enable the Office to pursue its vision of being “A Model Supreme Audit Institution that adds value to society” and its mission “To provide our stakeholders with independent audit results that promote good governance for better service delivery.” The strategic plan presents the aspirations to achieve enhanced organisational/ institutional performance and professionalism. This plan is designed to build upon the OAG’s success realised from the Corporate strategy 2016- 2021 which includes:executing 9,947 audits with improved quality from July 2016 to December 2019; strengthening collaborations and partnerships with stakeholders; and enhancing operational independence among others. It is worth noting that the corporate strategy 2016-2021 was reduced by one year to align with the National planning timelines. Pending activities from the corporate strategy 2016-2021 have been rolled over into this strategic plan. The development of this strategic plan was influenced by the Sustainable Development Goals, NDP III priorities, the Office’s internal performance assessment, and feedback from key stakeholders. To achieve office – wide congruence; this strategic plan has one goal, “Enhanced organizational performance for impactful audits”. This will be achieved through two strategic objectives 1- Enhance the relevance of audits for improved public transparency, accountability, and service delivery, and 2- Enhance institutional capacity to effectively and efficiently deliver the OAG’s mandate. Specific objectives, interventions, and activities have been developed to facilitate the achievement of these strategic objectives. This strategic plan intends to realize high impact audits that will enhance service delivery for the betterment of society as well as improving stakeholder satisfaction and the Office’s influence in the wider INTOSAI community. This strategy will be financed by the Government of Uganda (GoU) and Development Partners. Page 9 strategic report 1.0 INTRODUCTION 1.1. Overview of the Strategic Plan 2020 – 2025 The National Planning Authority Regulations 2018 (Section 18(1)) require all MDAs to prepare Strategic Plans in line with respective sector development plans and the medium term national development plan. The Office of the Auditor General developed a new strategic plan for the period 2020 – 2025 in line with the NDP III and the new Programmatic Approach to implementation of government activities/projects. The OAG Strategic Plan 2020 – 2025 is the fifth of its kind to be implemented by the office. Of the four previous strategic plans, three were implemented during/ after enactment of the NAA 2008. These covered the periods of; 2006 -2011, 2011-16 and 2016- 2021. This strategic plan was developed through a consultative process, by a Taskforce comprising staff from across the office. This process was supported by GIZ. In formulation of this Strategic Plan, the office made reference to the provisions of Uganda Vision 2040 as well as other Overarching Policy frameworks in consideration of the wider regional and international development planning context. These include: Agenda 2030 and the Sustainable Development Goals; Africa Agenda 2063; and the EAC Vision 2050. Page 10 strategic report The overall purpose of this 5 – year plan is to provide a comprehensive strategic direction that enables the Office of the Auditor General to meet the obligations of its mandate successfully and in line with the Vision, Mission, OAG strategic priorities and the NDP III while demonstrating sustainable value and relevance to the citizens. The Strategic Plan also sets out to provide a point of reference as the office navigates a constantly evolving operating environment. The National Goal spelt out in the NDP III is “To increase average household incomes and improve the quality of life of all Ugandans.” In conceptualizing a new Strategic direction to propel the office towards making a tangible contribution to the overall goal of the NDP III, the Office reviewed and updated its vision, Mission statement and Core values. The Plan therefore, is anchored on a new long term outlook which reflects the ambition of the office towards producing high quality audits effectively and efficiently with a view to delivering sustainable outcomes in public sector governance. This Plan consists of one overall goal and two strategic objectives that have been articulated to guide the office in enhancing institutional capacity to produce audits that add value to society. The Plan is further cascaded down into 7 specific objectives and 27 broad interventions. The new plan follows the last Corporate Strategy 2016 – 2021 whose implementation span was reduced by one year for purposes of alignment to the National development planning timelines and implementation horizon. In the process of aligning the Strategic Plan with the National Priorities laid out in the NDP III and PIAPs, key interventions from the previous strategic period that are still relevant were rolled over and included as undertakings in this Plan. The new Strategic Plan covers the period July 2020 – June 2025. Page 11 strategic report The Office of the Auditor General (OAG) is the Supreme Audit Institution (SAI) of Uganda. Following the enactment of the National Audit Act, 2008, it became a Corporate body. The SAI is headed by the Auditor General appointed by the President with the approval of Parliament under Article 163(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda 1995, as amended. The Auditor General’s mandate under Article 163(3) of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, 1995 as amended and ampliﬁed by Sections 13(1) of the National Audit Act (NAA) 2008, is to audit and report on the Public Accounts of Uganda and all public oﬃces including the courts, the central and local Government Administrations, Universities and Public Institutions of like nature, and any Public Corporations or other bodies established by an Act of Parliament. In addition, Article 163(3)(b) of the Constitution requires the Auditor General to conduct ﬁnancial and value for money audits in respect to any project involving public funds, while Article 163(4) requires him or her to submit to Parliament a report of the accounts audited by him or her for the ﬁnancial year immediately preceding and audits undertaken. Article 154(3) requires the Auditor General to approve the withdrawal of funds from the consolidated fund as prescribed by Parliament. Furthermore, Section 19(2) of the NAA, 2008 as amended by Section 82(4), of the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA) 2015, requires the Auditor General to audit and report to Parliament within six (6) months after the end of the ﬁnancial year. 1.2. Background and Legal framework Page 12 strategic report The functions and powers of the Auditor General 1.3. Geographical Coverage of the Office of the Auditor General The functions and powers of the Auditor General as specified in Part III of the National Audit Act 2008 and the Public Financial Management Act 2015 include: The headquarters of the OAG are located at Audit House, Plot 2C Apollo Kagwa road, Kampala and it also accommodates Kampala branch office. Other branch offices are located in Gulu, Fort portal, Mbarara, Masaka, Mbale, Soroti, Jinja, Arua, Kampala, Hoima and Moroto. 1. Approve withdrawal of funds from the Consolidated Fund. 2. Audit and report on the public accounts of Uganda and all public oﬃces, including; a. Audit of accounts of the central government. b. Audit of accounts of local government councils and administrative units. c. Audit of accounts of public organisations. d. Audit of public monies in private organisations and bodies. e. Certiﬁcation and report on the audit. f. Refer to the appropriate committee of Parliament any non-compliance, deﬁciency and none attainment of value for money. g. Conduct Value for Money audits. h. Conduct special audits and investigations i. Engage private auditors to assist him or her in the performance of his or her functions. j. Recommend to Parliament that a person in default or responsible for any loss or deficiency established in the course of audit show cause why he or she should not be surcharged with the amount. k. Make recommendations to the Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED) to minimize unproductive expenditure and maximize revenues, as well as averting any loss. l. Grant warrants for the withdrawal of funds from the Petroleum Fund. Page 13 strategic report 1.4. Organisational structure: The Office structure provides for two divisions namely Audit and Corporate Services Divisions. The Audit Division is comprised of five directorates namely: Central Government One; Central Government Two; Local Authorities; Value for Money and Specialised Audits; Forensic Investigations and Information Technology Audits. The Corporate Services division consists of Corporate Support and Technical Support Directorates. Refer to the detailed organisational structure in Annex 2. Page 14 strategic report 1.5 OAG value addition process (OAG Business Model) Figure 1: OAG Business model The OAG business model is deﬁned by the institutional legal framework, organisational systems, and processes, outputs, as well as resultant value and beneﬁts to society. The Office undertakes audits aimed at adding value by improving accountability, transparency, and good governance in Government service delivery processes and thus contributing to the enhancement of societal livelihood. Our audit processes follow applicable International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAIs) and internally developed guidelines. In line with her mandate, the Office undertakes financial, compliance, value for money, specialised and information technology audits, as well as forensic investigations and special audits upon request by stakeholders. Figure 2: Accountability cycle As illustrated above, Parliament provides the mandate and discusses the Auditor General’s report in executing its oversight role, whereas the Executive provides resources (budget) to the Auditor General and in turn, the Auditor General provides audit assurance on management of resources. In this process, consultations with stakeholders are critical to identifying risks and areas of interest at the planning stage. Entry meetings are held to discuss the Audit plan with the clients, audits are executed and exit meetings are held to discuss the findings with management to ensure; objectivity and fair hearing, understanding of audit issues raised, and recommendations thereof. As part of reporting for financial and compliance audits, final management letters and reports with the opinion of the Auditor General are issued to those charged with management. Final reports are also issued for other types of audits to those charged with governance and other predetermined stakeholders. Exercises propriety and prudence in publics spending Parliament Executive Make policy submit budget Approve and allocate funds Provide mandate Audit accounts & Report Implement policies and execute programmes Auditor General Implement policies and execute programmes Page 16 strategic report The Accountability value chain as provided for by various pieces of legislation has four steps namely: Planning and Budgeting, Implementation, Audit and Oversight, and Follow-up of Parliament’s recommendations to the executive through the audit of Treasury Memoranda. An illustration of the value chain in the accountability cycle. Figure 3: Value chain in the Accountability cycle 1.6. Strategic planning process for the period 2020-2025 i. Purpose of the Strategic Plan ii. Process of developing the Strategic Plan This Strategic plan is one of the core policy documents that define the strategic direction of the OAG and sets performance benchmarks for five years from Financial Year (FY) 2020/21 to FY 2024/25. It defines the goal, objectives and structures to deliver our obligations and responsibilities under the National Development Plan (NDP III) and the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda 1995 as amended. Our strategic objectives, interventions, and activities have been annualised to ease implementation and monitoring. A task force comprising of 14 members of the OAG supported by representatives from the National Planning Authority and Office of the Prime Minister developed this plan. The process included a review of the Legal framework, 2016-2021 Corporate Strategy 3 and a half year evaluation report, 2019 Institutional Capacity Building Self-assessment report, Institution quality assurance and audit reports, and the 2017 Supreme Audit Institutions performance measurement framework report. The process also involved consultation with Stakeholders, OAG leadership and Staff, Development Partners, Parliament, Civil Society and Media among others. Structure of the strategic plan The strategic plan is arranged in a logical order to provide the user with information to understand the OAG’s contribution to improving accountability and good governance, structures to deliver this plan, costed strategic intent, and monitoring and evaluation arrangements as indicated below; 1.0: Overview of the plan. 2.0: Situational analysis 3.0: Strategic Direction 4.0: Financing framework and Strategy 5.0: Institutional Arrangements for Implementing the Plan 6.0: Monitoring and Evaluation procedures 7.0 Risk Management 8.0: Communication and Feedback mechanisms 9.0: Project Profiles Formation of a task force, development of the Terms of reference and concept paper. Phase 1 Development of strategic intent by those charged with OAG Governance Phase 2 Literature review Review of assessment reports. Stakeholder analysis and consultation. Data analysis and development of Vision, Mission and Core Values. Phase 3 Development of Objectives, strategies, Costed implementation plan, Monitoring and Evaluation results framework and Validation with stakeholders. Phase 4 Approval of strategic plan by Top Management, Sub committee on Finance and budget of Parliament Awareness activities to stakeholders. Phase 5 Page 18 strategic report Existing Legal frameworks This strategic Plan takes into account the requirements of existing National and International laws. Good governance Resource availability Sustainability of the initiatives Stakeholder partnerships and relations Stable macroeconomic environment Effective Monitoring and Evaluation system Positive exercise of authority in promoting accountability, management of feedback, prudent handling of emerging risks, upholding the organisation’s norms and values as well as instilling and encouraging a culture of high performance will lead to successful implementation. Mobilisation of adequate resources to finance the plan is essential for its successful implementation. Alignment of the strategic plan to the NDP III and adoption of the SDGs within the OAG operating framework, as well as prudent and balanced implementation is a prerequisite for its sustainable realisation. Successful implementation of this plan requires strong partnerships and collaboration with stakeholders. The OAG will continuously strengthen and widen its scope of stakeholder engagements to enhance performance. The operating environment of the OAG is significantly influenced by prevailing macroeconomic factors, which have a bearing on the resource envelope and audit strategies. Such factors include inflation rate, exchange rates, macroeconomic policies, and general influences on economic growth among others. A stable macroeconomic environment is an enabler for the successful implementation of the strategic plan. Continuous assessment of and soliciting feedback on the performance of the strategic plan is a critical factor towards realisation of its goal and objectives. This will support evidence-based decision-making and the adoption of corrective measures. iv. Guiding Principles of the plan Strong leadership role For any plan to be successfully implemented, it requires a firm tone and involvement from Management. Continuous reflection and guidance on implementing initiatives will create ownership and congruence in attaining the goal and objectives set in this plan. Page 19 strategic report 2.1. Performance of the 2016-2021 Corporate Strategy as at 31st December 2019 Figure 5: Performance of strategic Objectives per goal The overall performance of the corporate strategy for the three and half years ending 31st December 2019 was as follows; 37% of combined strategic activities were completed, 57% were in progress and 6% were not started. This was partly due to the reduction of the corporate strategy period by one year to 30th June 2020 instead of 30th June 2021 to align it with NDP II and III timelines. Key milestones for the above goals During the above implementation period, the Office made significant improvements in performance as highlighted below: i. In line with the Auditor General’s mandate, the Office delivered the audits highlighted in the table below: Type of audit 2011 -2016 (five years) 2016-2020 (four years) Remarks Financial audits 8,313 9,107 This includes audits of the Consolidated Government of Uganda Financial Statements, Central Government Ministries Departments and Agencies (MDAs), Projects, Public Universities, Uganda Missions abroad, Commissions, National Referral Hospitals, Higher Local Governments, Urban councils, Sub Counties, Schools, and Tertiary Institutions Value for Money audits 53 38 These are independent examinations of the extent to which a public organisation has used its resources in carrying out its responsibilities in line with the principles of economy, efficiency, and effectiveness. The Office adopted INTOSAI standards by implementing the Financial Audit Methodology (FAM) and the Compliance Audit Methodology (CAM) as part of continued efforts to improve audit processes. Table 1: Audits conducted during the strategic periods 2011-2016 and 2016-2020 Page 21 strategic report b. Success factors that influenced the last Corporate Strategy 2016-202 Parliamentary Support. Leadership and Management commitment Support from Development Partners. OAG’s strong partnership with Parliament in fulfilling its role to oversee public accountability enhanced our performance. Parliament’s support towards financing the Office, discussing audit reports and following up audit recommendations in discharging its oversight function, and its continuous guidance influenced improvements in our performance. Development Partners’ support towards improving operational independence and the OAG’s capacity to effectively contribute to improving public accountability and service delivery to the citizens requires recognition. With their support, the Office has achieved significant advancements in pysical independence and capacity building. OAG’s leadership and management commitment was an engine in driving the performance of the corporate strategy. Their tireless efforts to guide implementation of the initiatives and establishment of a Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting function to continuously assess the performance of the strategy cannot be over-emphasized. vii. The Office enhanced its operational independence by constructing and equipping Hoima and Moroto branch offices increasing our branch offices from 9 to 11. Arua branch reconstruction is ongoing and is expected to be completed by the end of 2020. The Office has also acquired 5 acres of land expected to accommodate a training centre, host Kampala branch office and forensic laboratories. viii. To improve efficiency and effectiveness, the Office secured funding and completed the procurement process for an Integrated Management Information System. Its implementation commenced in the FY 2020/2021. ix. In addition, the Office undertook a job evaluation exercise that comprised a review of the organisation structure, job grading, and designing job descriptions for all positions. Implementation of the Job Evaluation recommendations is in progress. x. The Office strengthened its relationship with other stakeholders in the accountability sector. In this regard, the Office signed three MoUs namely: OAG, PPDA, and IG; OAG and URA; and lastly OAG and FIA to share information and improve the delivery of each institution’s respective mandate. xi. The Office continues to contribute to the international community by chairing and hosting the secretariat of INTOSAI Working Group on Audit of Extractive Industries (WGEI). Besides, our relationship with INTOSAI affiliated bodies such as AFROSAI-E has been strengthened. Page 22 strategic report c. Challenges in implementing the previous Corporate Strategy Measurement of results Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) Alignment of OAG Corporate Strategy timelines to NDP II The absence of baseline information, milestones - evaluating progress over time and measurable performance indicators in the corporate strategy made it difficult to assess the outcomes. The strategy was ambitious and lacked a clear and appropriate M&E framework to monitor and track implementation. In addition, the late establishment of the Monitoring and Evaluation Unit to monitor, evaluate, and report on the implementation of the strategy hampered the feedback system and follow up of implementation. The OAG corporate strategy 2016-2021 planning period was not aligned to the National Development Plan (NDPII) due to historic Office planning cycles that started before the National Planning Authority produced the country’s first NDP I. As a result, the strategy-implementing period was reduced from 5 to 4 years to ensure alignment of the implementation period with the NDP III. Roles and responsibilities in the corporate strategy were assigned at a high-level i.e. Assistant Auditor General-Audit and Assistant Auditor General-Corporate; as a result, the Directorates, Departments, and Units did not take ownership and direct responsibility for implementing the strategy. The above limitations have been considered in the formulation of this strategic plan 2020 – 2025. The post strategic planning activities will involve awareness engagements with all stakeholders to continuously collect performance data and feedback for management to take corrective actions. Improved human resource capacity. During the period, our workforce increased from 457 staff in 2016 to 531 staff in 2019. The capacity building initiatives supported by GoU, Development partners, and peer Supreme Audit Institutions enhanced professionalism, motivation, and commitment to deliver on the Office’s mandate. The youthful staff have been fundamental in coping with an increased workload in the dynamic environment. Page 25 strategic report The OAG contributes to the attainment of the United Nations SDGs through the audits we undertake. Our financial audits touch on several SDGs, but mainly cover SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions). The forensic investigations, Value for Money, Specialized and compliance audits consider several aspects of the SDGs following the Office’s priority themes and overall risks. Page 27 strategic report A chart illustrating the progression of OAG women versus Men per age group Figure 6: Progression of OAG women against Men per age group as at 31st December 2020 2.5. Description of cross-cutting issues impacting on Accountability, Transparency and Good Governance Gender and Equity Article 21(1) to (3) of The Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, 1995 (as amended), guarantees equality and freedom from discrimination of all persons under the law. Gender mainstreaming is a Government framework initiative for redressing gender imbalances. As a result, a National Gender policy (2007) was formulated and it requires that planning, resource allocation, and implementation of development programmes have a gender perspective. In line with the above and SDG 5 (achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls), the OAG Human Resource Manual and policy (2013) advocates for the principle of equal opportunities for all employees regarding recruitment, selection and promotions, remuneration, training and staff development, welfare, deployment, working environment and managerial decision making. The office is cognizant of gender balance and has hence improved gradually to 65% (346) Male and 35% (185) female as at December 2019. The top management composition of females currently stands at 24%. All staff members are treated justly without discrimination. OAG gender mainstreaming has been progressing as indicated in the chart below. Page 28 strategic report The majority of the women being in the youthful and productive age group require more support to balance the work requirements and family demands. The OAG women initiated a program (OAG Women’s Forum) to promote, improve, and maintain the professional and social growth of women at all levels in 2008 to help and address the emerging challenges. The major objectives of the forum are: a. To create a platform for discussing gender-related challenges that directly or indirectly impact on the attainment of the OAG mission, vision, and core values. b. To create a platform for OAG women and other employees to engage in professional and career development initiatives thus enhancing their ability to work effectively and efficiently in the attainment of the OAG mission. The Office supports the forum’s workplan and facilitates its activities whenever funds are available. The Office is implementing the principles of gender and equity in budgeting and the development of its strategic and operational work plans. Additionally, the Office has mainstreamed gender and equity in all its activities. During this strategic implementation period, the following interventions towards enhancing gender and equity will be pursued; i. A staff satisfaction survey aggregated by gender shall be undertaken and recommendations therein will be considered ii. Improving mothers’ welfare by providing child daycare facilities after constructing an off-site facility and freeing up space at Audit House. iii. Integrating gender and equity in human resource management and encouraging men to actively participate in gender-related initiatives. HIV/AIDS The Constitution of the Republic of Uganda 1995, as amended contains some provisions that guide and influence the management of the national response to HIV/AIDS particularly the roles and mandates of government structures at various levels, protection of the rights of citizens and provision of social and economic services. Since the Government declared HIV/AIDS to be a threat to national development, efforts have been made to mainstream HIV/AIDS in national development frameworks and other sector-related strategies. The Office recognizes HIV/AIDS as a serious threat and takes all necessary measures towards its prevention, mitigation, and control, these include; Continous implementation of a non-discriminatory HIV/AIDS policy (2013) by promoting the health and productivity of staff members through developing and implementing effective prevention and care strategies for staff and immediate families guided by the following principles; Page 29 strategic report i. Equal rights, opportunities, and obligations ii. Protection against discrimination iii. Access to complete information, education, and communication iv. Confidentiality In addition, the Office plans to acquire professional counseling services accessible to all staff to ensure healthy and productive lives. Environment The Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, 1995 (as amended) under national objectives and directive principles of state policy Item XVII provides for sustainable utilization of natural resources in a balanced manner for the present and future generations. Article 39 provides that every Ugandan has a right to a clean and healthy environment. In line with the above provisions, the Office has developed the capacity to undertake environmental audits and as such, the Office produces one environmental audit report annually. Also, the Office is a member of the INTOSAI Working Group on Environmental Auditing (WGEA) and continues to participate in WGEA activities. i. Increasing staff awareness on environmental issues about climate change and benefits of improving and preservation of a good environment for the future. ii. Reduce carbon emission by reducing paperwork through the digitalization of all Office business processes as well as introducing environment-friendly lighting systems to reduce energy consumption. Proposals are being considered to introduce sensor-controlled water dispersers. iii. As part of our commitment to improving the environment, the Office will participate in the International Environmental day on 5th June every year. The Office plans to enhance its responsiveness to environmental matters by; Innovation The NDP III Objective 5 requires the Government to initiate interventions to increase transparency and eliminate corruption in the delivery of services through automation of institutional management function by strengthening e-Government. In this regard, the Office uses Teammate audit software to execute its audit processes. Additionally the Office uses an official website to disseminate audit reports and other information to the public and intranet within the Office, as part of the effort to promote transparency and accountability. The Office will be automating its business processes through an Integrated Management Information System project and develop a shared platform to disseminate and follow up audit recommendations. Page 30 strategic report Corruption, Culture and Mind-set The National Development Plan III Objective 5 requires the Government to initiate interventions to improve transparency and accountability systems through strengthening the prevention, detection, and elimination of corruption. OAG’s contribution towards the above requirement has been through audits (financial, compliance, value for money, specialised audits, and forensic investigation audits). We have also participated in anti-corruption awareness campaigns through media, barazas, and charity walks among others. The Office is also committed to upholding ethical values and inculcating a culture of accountability in its business processes. We plan to enhance the above interventions by implementing the following; i. Introduce and implement mechanisms to prevent and fight corruption by enabling whistleblowing, investigation and follow up of corruption cases ii. Implement inclusive, transparent, and holistic planning and performance reporting iii. Deepening of audits targeting corruption as well as strengthening collaboration with other anti- corruption institutions. 2.6. Summary of emerging issues and implications E-Government The Government has been implementing e-Government initiatives to promote transparency and accountability. Such initiatives include the Integrated Financial Management System, Integrated Payroll Management System, University IT Systems, URA revenue IT management System, and National ID project among others. In addition, the Government has prioritized automation of institutional management functions under the National Development Plan III - Public Sector transformation programme, Objective 5 to increase transparency and eliminate corruption in the delivery of services. To effectively deliver the audit mandate, the Office will be required to enhance its current capacity to cope with the changing e-governance environment. The improvements will include increasing the number of IT auditors, enhancing skills, and retooling among others. Increased Government investment in infrastructure for production The country’s investment in infrastructure development such as the construction of roads and bridges, dams, and standard gauge railway among others has been growing over time. For instance, development expenditure on roads alone grew from UGX1.3 trillion in FY2013/14 to Page 31 strategic report Sustainability of National debt The country’s debt has been growing significantly. For example, public debt increased by 22% from UGX 33.99 trillion as at 30th June 2017 to UGX 41.51 trillion by 30th June 2018. Although Uganda’s debt to GDP ratio is still below the IMF risky threshold of 50%, it is unfavorable when debt payment is compared to National revenue collected which was the highest in the region at 51%3 at the end of FY2017/18. This indicates increased country dependence on borrowing, a rise in concerns about debt sustainability, and a reduction in sovereign credit rating. Audit of debt acquisition and management, as well as expenditure of borrowed funds, presents a challenge as it requires specialised skills to understand the borrowing processes and contracts. This calls for improved staff capacity to monitor and audit national debt. 2 Background to the budget Fiscal Year 2018/19 3 Annual report of the Auditor General for FY2017/18 4 Uganda Oil and Gas brochure April 2019 Uganda’s Oil and Gas sector has transitioned from exploration to preparation of discovered oil fields for production (development) and putting in place infrastructure for commercial production of the discovered 6 Billion barrels of oil and gas resources and facilitating developments in the sector4. In addition, Uganda’s Vision 2040 aims to promote local beneficiation through value addition to minerals, in line with UN Agenda 2030 and AU Agenda 2063 which aim to achieve the sustainable management and efficient use of natural resources. SAI Uganda as a member of INTOSAI chairs the Working Group on Audit of Extractive Industries. This presents an opportunity to build capacity through knowledge sharing with other members of INTOSAI. The OAG has continued to build capacity in the audit of extractive industries. However, there has been a high turnover of skilled staff that has joined other government bodies in the sector. Furthermore, as noted above the sector has evolved and requires enhanced skills to undertake audits in exploration, infrastructure development, production, and sales. Uganda became a member of the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI) and the Office was appointed EITI-Uganda information auditor. Extractive Industries UGX1.7 trillion in FY2017/182. Infrastructure development remains an area of focus in NDP III as it plays an important role in contributing to a higher rate of economic growth leading to improvement of the country’s standard of living. The mandate of the Auditor General is to assure that public resources have been prudently utilized in delivering the above projects. To achieve this, engineering and other specialised audits must be conducted. The increase in infrastructure investments requires enhanced OAG capacity to deliver the assurance required. Page 32 strategic report Natural disasters and country preparedness The recent spate of natural disasters across the country for example landslides, floods, prolonged droughts and locust invasions have contributed to retardation of the country’s growth and development. These disasters have led to loss of lives and property as well as a decline in the livelihood of affected communities. The country’s disaster interventions in addition to coordination of relief and resettlement of affected persons, increases the strain on the National budget and remains a high-risk audit area. Successful audit of this sector will require sufficient capacity to undertake audits at all levels of the extractive industries value chain. This will necessitate attracting appropriately skilled staff and enhancing the capacity of existing staff to undertake such audits as well as designing initiatives to reward and retain them. Corona Virus Pandemic (COVID-19) Impact The emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic without a cure or vaccine has disrupted economic activities worldwide. The duration of the pandemic is not foreseeable and its impact may not be easily measured and ascertained. Its spread has interrupted and changed our way of living and work. There is a need to innovate and adopt new methods of working while complying with prevention guidelines. The process of adopting new methods will take a while hence slowing down the current productivity of staff as well as increasing the use and cost of ICT infrastructure. Contingency planning shall be integrated into our management practices. 2.7. Institutional capacity: Government of Uganda funding Financial Resources: The GoU budget provision increased from UGX 46.496Bn in 2015/2016 to UGX 66.136Bn in 2019/2020 (including in–year supplementary allocations) representing an increase of 39.24% over the 5 year span. Over the five year period, the average release vis-à-vis the approved budget was 99.23% while the average 5 year absorption rate (expenditure vis-à-vis release) was 99.05%. Over the past five financial years (FYs 2015/2016 to 2019/2020), the Office received funding from two primary sources namely: the Government of Uganda and support from Development Partners. The GoU funding together with Development Partners support resulted in enhanced performance notably reflected by an increase from 1711 audits in 2016 to 3316 in 2019. Page 33 strategic report The graph below shows the year-by-year budgetary allocation to the OAG. Figure 7: Year-by-Year budgetary allocation to the OAG Support from Development partners OAG received support from FINMAP and REAP equivalent to UGX11.794 Bn for improving institutional capacity and operational independence by constructing and equipping Hoima, Moroto, and Arua branch offices as well as supporting the procurement of an Integrated Management Information System (IMIS), among others. European Union supported the Office with UGX9Bn to undertake infrastructure and LLG backlog audits and to build staff capacity in various disciplines. In addition, GAPP/USAID contributed UGX108Mn towards processing LLG backlog reports. The Office received technical support from peer SAIs (Norway and Sweden) towards enhancing the quality of audits and communicating audit results. GIZ has been providing technical assistance to OAG since 2013. The support includes improving Office systems and structures, general capacity building, and enhancing stakeholder management and collaborations. The SAI is a developing organization that requires continuous enhancement of its capacity to cope with changing audit standards, emerging issues and evolving stakeholder’s interests in delivering the mandate. Page 34 strategic report Human Resources: Our human resource is invaluable in delivering the audit mandate and our successful performance depends on the skills and experience posessed by our staff. In addition, our workforce is diverse representing all ages, affiliations and backgrounds of our society. The Office continues to support its staff through training and development to ensure that they are sufficiently empowered to deliver the mandate and unlock their potential. OAG has qualified staff who possess a vast range of skills across various professions including Accountants, Statisticians, Engineers, Economists, Geologists, Social Scientists, Environmentalists, IT specialists and Lawyers. The total establishment for the OAG stands at 527 out of which, only 484 positions are filled. This translates to a nine percent (9%) staffing gap. 386 staff are deployed in the audit directorates as technical staff and 98 staff in the corporate division provide support to the audit function of the office. Majority of the staff (34.9% overall and 44% of the audit staff) are deployed in Local Authorities to enhance access to audit services across the country as shown in the figure below. Figure showing staff deployment across the different directorates. Figure 9: Staff deployment across the different directorates. Page 35 strategic report Monitoring and Evaluation Function: Accountability and transparency are essential elements of good governance arrangements and the OAG holds these pillars in high regard. As a consequence, the office keeps reviewing its own operations and performance with an aim to achieve higher standards than the organisations it audits. The OAG has a functional monitoring and evaluation unit currently headed by a Senior M&E officer supported by a Monitoring and Evaluation Officer. The unit is guided by the National M&E Policy 2013, OAG M&E Policy, M&E Framework and OAG M&E guidelines. The function scopes its work to continuously report on a quarterly and annual basis. The quarterly reports focus on the annual operational plans implementing the strategic plan whereas the annual report focuses on the overall performance for the financial year. Following the policy, the M&E unit reports to the M&E committee for quality control and assurance and subsequently, submits its report to Top management through the Director responsible. The annual performance reports are also submitted to the subcommittee of Parliament on Finance, Planning and Economic development which oversees OAG governance. In addition, budget performance reports are generated from the Programme Budgeting System (PBS) and submitted to MoPFED as required by the PFMA 2015. All M&E data and information is subjected to review and quality assurance checks to preserve the integrity of the data generated annually before publication of any M&E result. Our Vision, Mission, and Core Values Our vision: - ‘A model Supreme Audit Institution that adds value to society.’ Our core values: In carrying out our responsibilities and work, we are guided and committed to living by our core values below: Integrity and Ethical conduct: Being honest and morally upright. Professional competence: To act with diligence, proficiency, and team spirit. Objectivity: Being impartial. Service – delivery oriented: Value addition centered. Our mission: - ‘To provide our stakeholders with independent audit results that promote good governance for better service delivery.’ 3.3. OAG Strategic Goal, Objectives and Outcomes Overall goal: Enhanced organizational performance for impactful audits The strategic focus for the period 2020-2025 is to make a sustainable difference in the lives of citizens and add value to society. The Office has prioritized improved organizational performance in all operational aspects through 2 strategic objectives: 1 -Enhance the relevance of audits for improved public transparency, accountability, and service delivery; and 2 - Enhance institutional capacity to effectively and efficiently deliver its mandate. Consequently, the envisioned performance gains arising from the planned strategic objectives are geared towards the realisation of relevant and high impact audits that will enhance service delivery for the betterment of society as well as improved stakeholder satisfaction and the office’s influence in the wider INTOSAI community. This strategy is designed to build upon the OAG’s past successes while taking into account current and emerging issues related to public accountability and good governance. Consultation with stakeholders and our performance assessment provided a clear understanding of the objectives for this strategic plan. Interventions to address Cross – cutting issues In development of this Strategic Plan, specific reference was made to other key overarching Policy Frameworks. These include: Vision 2040, Africa Agenda 2063, Agenda 2030 (Sustainable Development Goals) and the EAC Vision 2050. Therefore, the formulation of the overall strategic direction was done with the deliberate intention of creating a clear linkage to the provisions in these frameworks. Additionally, the office through execution of its audits that provide assurance on the utilization of public resources, makes a direct contribution to achievement of all the objectives in these policy frameworks as well as implementation of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals. Page 49 strategic report 4.0 FINANCING FRAMEWORK AND STRATEGY 4.1. Costing interventions and results 4.2. Summary of funding requirements and MTEF projections (Billions) Interventions under corporate strategy 2016 - 2021 were financed with support from GOU and Development Partners as indicated in section 2.7 above. The costing of this strategic plan has been done consultatively across the Office taking into account the different resource requirements necessary for the realisation of the strategic objectives set forth. In the next five-year strategic period, the Office shall still require support from the Government of Uganda and Development Partners. Determination of related costs in this strategic plan has been guided by the following assumptions: Inflation and market prices will not change significantly; Foreign exchange rate shall not exceed UGX 3,900 to 1 USD; Public Service guidance on duty facilitation allowances shall not change; and MTEFs shall remain as projected. The total funding requirement to finance this strategic plan over the five years is UGX 469Bn. It is envisaged that this Strategic Plan shall be primarily financed by Government of Uganda and Development Partners, as has been the case in the previous strategic periods. Audit of self-financing government bodies OAG being a member of INTOSAI will continue to subscribe to their capacity-building programmes to enhance institutional and human resource capacity to deliver the Office mandate and add value to society. INTOSAI develops audit standards for SAIs and delivers capacity programmes through its affiliated bodies. Consequently, OAG will continue to strengthen its partnership with INTOSAI and its affiliated bodies especially AFROSAI-E. The Auditor-General will continue to undertake audits in such Government bodies as required by law. Outsourced audit firms appointed by the Auditor General through tripartite arrangement sometimes audit these organisations. These organisations budget and pay fees for the audit services directly to the audit firms. However, some organisations have challenges financing the audits. OAG will enhance its coordination with these self-financing organisations to prioritize audit funding under section 30 of the NAA 2008. Page 52 strategic report 5.0 INSTITUTIONAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR IMPLEMENTING THE PLAN 5.1 Coordination arrangements The Auditor General has the overall responsibility of delivering this strategic plan; whereas the Assistant Auditor General-Audit and his/her Directors are responsible for realizing strategic objective 1-Enhance the relevance of audits for improved public transparency, accountability, and service delivery; and the Assistant Auditor General-Corporate with his/her Directors will be responsible for delivering strategic objective 2 - Enhance institutional capacity to effectively and efficiently deliver its mandate. The implementation of the strategic plan will be through established OAG organisational structures, specifically the responsibility centres identified in the implementation matrix. Roles and responsibilities of key stakeholders in implementation of the strategic plan are indicated in Annex 8. a. Independence and Legal framework: This Strategic Plan has prioritized review of the National Audit Act 2008 and Article 163 and 164 of the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda 1995 (as Amended) as one of the key deliverables during the strategic period 2020 – 2025. This will provide the framework to enhance the independence of the Auditor General, to create an enabling environment to ensure the Office 5.2 Sustainability Arrangements The OAG Strategic plan 2020 – 2025 aims to effectively build institutional capacity to deliver the mandate of the Auditor General while adding value to society in the near and long term. The sustainability arrangements are highlighted below: Page 53 strategic report b. Governance (Leadership and management): The OAG Governance structures are a key area of focus as the drivers for the attainment of the long and medium-term goals of the OAG. Therefore, the OAG Strategic Plan 2020 – 2025 aims to improve on the robustness and operation of the governance arrangements at all levels, to ensure clarity of roles and responsibilities; promoting organizational transparency; improving internal controls and OAG systems; as well as efficient and effective management for results. c. Human resource capacity: In the development of the OAG Strategic Plan 2020 – 2025, the integral role of human resources has been accounted for. Our staff capacity is critical in achieving the objectives of the Office. Moving forward, the strategic plan aims to enhance the capacity to deliver the OAG mandate. To comply with ISSAIs, the Office is required to continuously equip its staff with the necessary skills, knowledge, and tools to undertake audits of varying complexity and in a changing environment. Additionally, the mandate and scope of audit have been increasing as a result of creating more government administrative structures, projects, and improving demand for accountability. Therefore, the OAG Strategic plan has emphasized building staff capacity at all levels to effectively execute its mandate and create a difference. can sustainably deliver its mandate. The legal and regulatory framework governing the Office should take into account dynamic circumstances and adequately provide for the Office to meet its obligations over time, and therefore the Office will pursue the steps necessary to realise this objective. d. Rationalization of resources: Effective management of resources is essential to the sustainability of the OAG. The Strategic Plan has taken into account the projected resource requirements for the strategic activities detailed in this plan over the next 5 years. Implementation of the Integrated Management Information System will improve efficiencies in our business processes. The Office plans to develop a policy on audit resource rationalisation, which will lead to focusing resources on high value and high impact audits. Besides, the plan provides for effective utilization of human resource to undertake audits in low peak periods (January to April) e. Innovations: In response to government priorities, specifically implementing E-governance, Extractive industries initiatives, and increasing investment in infrastructure, the Office has planned for activities to enhance its capacity through innovation by acquiring appropriate technologies and equipping staff with the necessary skills to undertake audits in the above priority areas. Office structures and systems encourage creativity and innovation. Page 54 strategic report f. Harnessing synergies from collaborations: The strategic plan has provided for strengthening collaborations along the accountability value chain and with external stakeholders to ensure the sustainability of Audit outcomes. This plan provides for enhancement of the collaboration with Parliament, the Executive (MDAs and LGs), and Anti-corruption agencies to sustainably harness synergies in promoting good public accountability and service delivery. In addition, the OAG as a member of INTOSAI and its affiliated bodies will strengthen its partnerships with other SAIs, Development Partners, Media, and Civil Society to build capacity and promote transparency and public accountability. g. Monitoring and evaluation: Availability of timely, reliable, and accurate information is essential for effective performance tracking and decision-making. An independent OAG M&E function has been established and critical interventions have been designed to enhance its capacity to effectively monitor and evaluate the implementation of this strategic plan. The Office shall continue to ingrain performance monitoring at all levels of the organization. This will foster a culture of accountability and high performance aimed at sustainably achieving the overall objectives. Page 55 strategic report 6.0 MONITORING AND EVALUATION PROCEDURES 6.1. Monitoring and Evaluation Procedures The OAG has a monitoring and evaluation function headed by a Senior M&E officer. In the reviewed structure, it will be headed by a Manager Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation. The function is guided by the National M&E Policy 2013, OAG M&E Policy and guidelines. This unit will spearhead the monitoring and evaluation of this strategic plan. The M & E team will independently conduct monitoring and evaluation activities and collaborate with other departments in creating awareness of the M&E function during this strategic planning period. In delivering the M&E function, the team will continuously engage the Planning unit to ensure that the annual work plans and budgets are aligned to the strategic plan. In collecting and validating performance information, engagements with Directorates,Departments and Units will be vital for ownership of the performance results and buy-in towards the implementation of recommendations therein. The engagements will also act as an avenue for assessment and providing feedback. 6.2. Progress Reporting In performing the M&E function, the team will report per the OAG structures, M&E Policy, and guidelines. The function will scope its work to continuously report on a monthly, quarterly and annual basis. The monthly and quarterly reports will focus on the annual operational plans implementing the strategic plan whereas the annual report will focus on the overall performance for the financial year. The annual performance reports will be published to demonstrate accountability and promote transparency. Page 56 strategic report 6.3. Annual Performance Review Following the annual performance report, review meetings will be held with different key stakeholders to evaluate the performance of the planned activities, identify challenges faced and suggest solutions, identify lessons learnt, key areas for improvement and discuss priorities for the subsequent year. 6.4. Midterm Evaluation 6.5. End Term Evaluation A mid-term evaluation will be conducted after two-and-half years (January 2023) of the plan’s implementation. The purpose of this evaluation will be to: assess progress on implementation of the set objectives; review the strategies to address emerging issues where necessary; discuss any hindrances and their mitigation to realise the targets; as well as lessons learnt. At the end of the implementation period, an End Term evaluation will be conducted to assess the realisation and sustainability of results. Following the policy, the M&E unit will report to the M&E committee for quality control and assurance and subsequently submit its report to Top management through the Director responsible. The annual performance reports will also be submitted to the subcommittee of Parliament overseeing OAG governance. In addition, budget performance reports will be generated from the Programme Budgeting System (PBS) and submitted to MoPFED as required by the PFMA 2015. Page 57 strategic report 7.0 RISK MANAGEMENT Office of the Auditor General operates in a dynamically evolving environment full of risks and uncertainty. This means that the planned activities could be significantly affected leading to inability to achieve our overall goal and objectives. It is therefore imperative that the office identifies enterprise risk and designs strategies to mitigate the impact of these risks. These strategies will continuously be monitored for adequacy during the implementation of the plan. Whilst the office can not entirely identify and eliminate all risks, being aware of the nature of these risks are and their origins can help us better manage their effect and steer a course to successful achievement of our objectives. The risks have been categorised as External, Strategic and Operational risks These are risks from uncertain and uncontrollable external events. External events that lead to external risk cannot be controlled by the office or cannot be forecasted with a high level of reliability. The office therefore has to take measures to reduce the impact of these risks. These are risks that the office accepts to execute the strategy in order to generate superior returns/long term benefits. They arise from the fundamental decisions that top management take concerning the office’s objectives. 7.1 Risk categories 7.1.1 External Risks 7.1.2 Strategic Risks: Page 58 strategic report These are risks arising from within the office’s operations that do not generate strategic or long-term benefit. They normally result from ineffective or failed internal processes, people and systems The AFROSAI-E Risk Management Guidelines require SAIs to take the necessary steps to identify, categorize and rank the risks it is exposed to according to their likely impact with the aim of taking a decision on how best the risks can be managed. The identified risks have been rated on a 3-band scale (i.e. High, Moderate, Low) and the respective responses required for each rating have been summarized in table 12 below. All risks have been compiled and presented in the risk matrix on Annex 9. The table presents the risk assessment and mitigation strategies for the identified strategic risks over the implementation of this Plan. In addition, activity level risks have also been detailed in the overall results framework (Annex 7) 7.1.3 Operational Risks: 7.2 Risk rating and compilation Table 12: Overall Risk Rating and Response Overall Rating (Impact x Likelihood) Response LOW: (1 – 2) Occasional monitoring. Tolerate; continue with existing mea­ sures and review annually. MODERATE: (3 – 5) Steady improvement needed. Continually monitor and perform periodic review. HIGH: (6 – 9) Highest priority, very serious concern. Immediate action re­ quired and review regularly. Page 59 strategic report 8.0 COMMUNICATION AND FEEDBACK MECHANISMS This strategic plan has been developed through a consultative process with staff at different levels as well as all directorates, departments, and units. It will be published on the Office website www. oag.go.ug and OAG intranet for accessibility by stakeholders and staff respectively. The hard copies will be printed and disseminated to selected stakeholders and public libraries. Awareness programmes of the strategic plan 2020-2025 will be designed to disseminate the strategic direction, interventions, and activities to all OAG departments and directorates including branches. This awareness will aim at providing insight into the changes and value that will be created by this strategic plan. It will also provide a platform for sensitizing staff on the transformation from merely providing assurance through auditing to a focus on adding value to society. Lastly, awareness will create ownership and buy-in to ease implementation. Implementation of the strategic plan has been sequenced across five financial years and this will inform the development of the annual budgets and work plans. These will be reviewed to assess the level of alignment to the NDP III and OAG strategic plan. This will subsequently create avenues for monitoring, evaluation, and obtaining feedback for improvement. Also, the strategic plan will be subjected to periodic reviews (annual, mid-term, and end-term) to assess the progress of implementation, identify and address emerging issues, and develop action logs to enhance performance. The mid and end-term evaluations will be conducted to take stock of achievements against the set objectives of the strategic plan. Page 60 strategic report 9.0 PROJECT PROFILES 9.1 OAG Integrated Management Information System (IMIS) The OAG Integrated Management Information System (IMIS) shall deliver improvement to the Office by: 1. Improving operational delivery and achievement of defined strategic KPI’s 2. Delivering better visibility around key departmental performance areas 3. Eliminating stand-alone operations across departmental business units 4. Achieving economies of scale & flexibility within the divisions 5. Curbing high costs related to resource acquisition & operational maintenance The Office is in the process of implementing the IMIS with support from KfW through REAP. This involves automation and integration of all OAG business processes onto one IT platform. To date, project governance structures have been established, change management initiatives are ongoing and related procurement processes have been undertaken. The contract was signed in September 2020 and its implementation is expected to start in October 2020. The contract value is UGX 32,750,664,205.32 (VAT inclusive). Page 61 strategic report Implementation Phases: For the IMIS, the contractor will provide consulting services covering the implementation of an SAP solution within the organization. The project will be implemented in five Phases of which Phase 0 is 4 months, Phase 1 is 8 months implementation and 2 months onsite Hyper care, Phase 2 is 6 months implementation and 2 months onsite hyper care, Phase 3 is 6 months implementation and 2 months onsite hyper care, Phase 4 is 5 months implementation and 2 months onsite hyper care. The total planned implementation period is 33 months. 9.2 Centre of Audit Excellence (Skills Enhancement Facility) Project Goal Project Justification To strengthen institutional capacity through high-quality capacity building programmes and establishing an engineering and forensic laboratory to enhance the quality and value of audits. The Government continues to invest heavily in infrastructure developments, e-governance, and extractives. This requires the OAG to attain adequate skills and tools to audit these priorities and emerging areas. Acquisition of such specialized skills is costly and the tools required need sufficient space for installation and on-site testing and analysis. Specialised skills and tools are particularly essential in non-financial audits such as engineering, VFM, IT, forensic, and Oil and gas. Establishing a Center of Audit Excellence will be a strategic opportunity to develop the audit profession in the specialized areas mentioned above and in any new areas that may arise over time both within Uganda and beyond. Key Processes of the Office that the IMIS shall address What modules / processes are going to be covered by the IMIS? Audit Management: Ensure the alignment of the organisational mission and vision to improve the use of TeamMate and ensure integration with the EDMS for centralized storage of the working papers as well as the other modules of the IMIS. Ensure that there is a clear synergy with the Audit process and related supporting corporate processes. Strategy and Planning Management: Ensure the alignment of the organisational mission and vision with a comprehensive score carding process, strategic goals, initiatives and objectives of the office. Procurement Management Process: To assist the OAG in archieving streamlined supplier management and the effective procurement processes in order to ensure compliance to legislation and regulation Asset and Inventory Management: To obtain a system of record that can help the OAG in managing the assets and inventory so as to utilize the resources more efficiently and thus improve on the delivery of services to staff in both divisions. Human Capital Management Improving capabilities and efficiencies around hire to retire processes Improving automation around employee self-service and training Key need for customized reporting and analytics Finance and Accounting Need for an integrated financial system with alignment to the long term strategic planning of OAG The financial system shall interface with the GOU IFMS system for reporting by the OAG. Governance, Risk and Compliance: Ensure the effective management of the OAG’s risk profile and mitigation strategies across all areas of the OAG and its business Project Perfomance Management: Key need to provide the office with a closed loop control system which deploys policy and strategy for all projects and programmers ran by the OAG IT Infrastructure Management: Need to replace all the equipment in the OAG Data Center as all existing equipment is End-Of-Life Integration of OAG into the National Data Centre and Disaster Recovery site Business Intelligence and Reporting: Requirement to collect complete and comprehensive data for analyzing, in order to help the OAG management team make better strategic and operational business decisions Electronic Document Management: Improving process efficiency in document management and retrieval Key requirements for access control to records and audit trail capability EDMS system should have native ERP & Project systems Page 62 strategic report Project Cost and Implementation Period The project is estimated to cost UGX 28.5 Bn and will be implemented over three years. 9.3 Development of A Shared Platform for Tracking Audit Recommendations Brief Project Background and Justification As part of the PFM reform strategy 2018-2023, the Government acknowledged the deficiencies regarding ascertaining the status of implementation of oversight recommendations. In response to the above, Government prioritized the establishment of an integrated system to track the status of external and internal recommendations arising from audits and investigations. This is to be operated on a shared platform with input from OAG, PPDA, Parliament, Internal Auditor General, Ministry of Local Government, Accountant General, Ministry of Public Service, and Office of the Prime Minister. Project Objectives Project financing and Implementation Period a. To engage key stakeholders’ instrumental for inducing implementation of audit recommendations to provide inputs for the establishment of the system b. To develop and implement a system for tracking all audit recommendations over five years. c. To build the capacity of those involved in manning the responsibility centers in the process of tracking the implementation of audit recommendations d. To provide timely feedback on the extent of implementation of audit recommendations to stakeholders for decision making. e. Designing a shared platform for tracking the status of implementation of recommendations for all participating Agencies. f. To assess impact of implemented audit recommendation over five years g. Customizing teammate software to capture recommendation implementation status as part of the routine audit process at the Accounting Officers’ level. This intervention is supported by REAP and will cost UGX 1.87Bn to develop an IT platform. The Office plans to invest UGX 306 million in other activities to effectively deliver the project. The project will be implemented over three years. The proposed facility will have: Modern training rooms; an auditorium with a capacity of at least 200 persons; board rooms; modern conference hall; document archival center; a back-up IT data center; Kampala regional branch office; engineering laboratory; forensic laboratory; recreational facilities; a resource center and storage facilities Page 63 strategic report Annexes 1.
